title: Hyperscaler managed endpoint seller brief
content:
Purpose:
Quick, tactical playbook for AEs and SEs selling Redwood against hyperscaler managed endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure). Focus: typical account questions, short rebuttals, demo checklist, cost/ops tradeoffs, and escalation signals. Not comprehensive — use for call prep and post-demo follow-ups.

TL;DR positioning hooks (one liners to use early):
- “We give you hyperscaler simplicity with platform-level control — so you get predictable latency and cost without building the ops stack yourself.”
- “Hyperscaler endpoints are great for dev access; Redwood is built for production inference economics and fallback resilience at scale.”
- “If you need private control plane, versioned rollouts, and token-level observability, the hyperscaler story gets patchy — we made those first-class.”

Competitor snapshot (what they sell vs where they struggle):
- AWS / SageMaker-like managed endpoints:
  - Strengths: deep infra ecosystem, integrated billing/identity, broad enterprise mindshare.
  - Weaknesses: endpoint models are often single-tenant abstractions over generic infra; limited automatic KV/prefix caching and limited model-specific batching heuristics out of the box. Latency SLOs are not tailored to LLM tail behavior. Egress and multi-region fallback are manual.
- GCP / Vertex-style endpoints:
  - Strengths: strong data/analytics integration, easy for Google-centric shops, good managed training/hosting pipeline.
  - Weaknesses: fewer precurated open model performance profiles, less opinionated runtime optimizations for LLMs (KV cache, quantization profiles). Observability is coarse for token-level cost attribution.
- Azure ML endpoints:
  - Strengths: enterprise compliance integrations, AD/Identity, and marketplace reach.
  - Weaknesses: heavy ops burden for multi-model routing/fallbacks and can require network plumbing for private deployments.

Where Redwood wins (concise themes):
- Production economics — observable unit cost + tuning: token-level cost breakdowns, batch sizing recommendations, and quantization profiles tied to real workload samples.
- Reliability & graceful degradation: automatic model fallback chains, cross-region routing, and transparent canary/rollback control plane.
- Unified experience across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private: same API + rollouts + tracing whether customer is on-hosted or on-prem.
- Developer-first ops: fast SDKs, traceable token attribution, and built-in eval/watchlists for quality regressions.
- Private & compliance posture without DIY: optional private control plane, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs — deployed and operated by Redwood for customers who can’t use hyperscaler managed endpoints unmodified.

Common customer objections and short rebuttals (use these verbatim):
- “We already use [cloud vendor], so using their endpoint is simpler.”
  - Rebuttal: “Totally — for early trials that’s the fastest path. At ~X% production traffic you start paying in inefficiencies (cold GPU hit, suboptimal batching, opaque token cost). We help teams migrate with a low-friction path that preserves dev velocity while improving unit economics and SLOs.”
- “Hyperscaler gives the same SLA / integration.”
  - Rebuttal: “They give infra-level SLA; they don’t give LLM-tailored SLAs (e.g., per-request latency under long-context and KV cache warm/cold scenarios). Redwood’s Dedicated SLA is tuned to LLM behavior — we guarantee throughput with smarter batching, cache warming, and fallback policies.”
- “We can just run on their VMs and manage it ourselves.”
  - Rebuttal: “You could, but that rebuilds the same operational complexity we’ve productized — kernel selection, quantization tuning, continuous batching, and model-specific runtime optimizations. Our platform saves months/heads for infra teams and a recurring ops tax thereafter.”

Pricing and economics counterpoints (what to ask and what to say):
- Ask: “What’s your current token throughput, peak qps, and percent p99 latency requirement?”
- Say: “Hyperscaler SUs/VMs often hide per-request cost patterns: cold starts, underutilized GPUs, and cross-region egress. We provide a modeled estimate: show them 3-month cost delta using their workload sample (we provide template). In many infra-bound workloads we see 20–45% TCO reduction after batching/cache/quantization.”
- Quick flex: Dedicated pools + autoscale + burst allows predictable committed capacity vs hyperscaler spotty VM autoscale behavior during regional contention.

Technical demo checklist (what SEs must show — 20 min focused demo script):
1) Live perf dashboard for a customer-like route: token cost, per-route latency, batching stats.
2) Canary rollout: deploy new model and show instant traffic split + automatic rollback when eval regressions spike.
3) Fallback in action: simulate capacity loss and show automatic model variant fallback with preserved API surface.
4) Private deployment highlight: KMS key rotation and audit log lookup in Console.
5) Cost tuning: change batching/quantization profile and show predicted vs actual cost delta.
6) Trace to token: show how a customer pinpoints a noisy prompt or hallucination via eval traces.

Account-specific discovery questions to surface hyperscaler vulnerability:
- Where does your data persist today? Do you need private control plane / data residency?
- How do you currently measure per-request token cost and attribute to business metrics?
- Do you have a dedicated infra team for model ops or are you hoping for self-serve?
- Peak QPS and target p99 latency SLAs? Cold start tolerance?
- Compliance: required certifications (SOC2, FedRAMP, regional requirements)?

Velocity and migration path (low friction play):
- Phase 0: PoC on Hosted API (mirror traffic from dev environment) — fast onboarding and sample performance profile.
- Phase 1: Shadow traffic to Dedicated — test fallback chains and billing attribution.
- Phase 2: Private control plane / VPC if required — verify KMS/HSM, routing, and audit logs.
- Notes: emphasize incremental approach — avoid ‘big-bang’ infra swaps. Provide migration checklist (routes, tokens, model versions).

Escalation / technical signals that mean we should loop in Product/Eng early:
- Customer demands sub-10ms token p99 at >500 qps sustained.
- They require a custom quantization kernel or exotic hardware not in our catalog.
- Network architecture demands (air-gapped on-prem) where the deployment shifts to Professional Services.

Suggested subject lines / short email snippets for AE outreach:
- Subject: “Reduce inference spend and get reliable p99 latency — quick example for [Acct]”
- Snippet: “We ran your sample prompt on a similar workload and saw 32% lower unit cost after caching and batching tweaks while improving p99 latency. Quick 20-min walkthrough?”

Open questions / backlog items (internal):
- Need a reference 1-pager with direct hyperscaler feature matrix (exact names, SLA language) — engineering input required (Action: Maya).
- Create a one-click sample-costing sheet in the Console for AEs to generate 3-month delta using customer token sample (Action: GH-PR-3891).
- Collect 3 anonymized case studies where we reduced TCO >25% vs hyperscaler baseline.

Quick rebuttal cheat-sheet (copy-paste):
- “Hyperscalers give end-to-end infra but not LLM-specific ops — we provide production LLM runtime features (caching, batching, model rollouts) as a service.”
- “If you need enterprise controls (KMS/HSM, private control plane) we can deliver that without your infra team owning the runtime.”

References and signals to include in deal notes:
- Links to workload traces, sample token histogram, and p99 baseline measurements.
- Note if the customer already has committed hyperscaler spend and whether they are open to multi-cloud or vendor-neutral approaches.

Unpolished notes / call fragments (for internal reuse):
- “Customer worried about egress costs — propose region-local Dedicated with VPC peering.”
- “They asked about model drift detection: demo our eval-watchlist and rollback.”
- TODO: consolidate pricing examples for 1M, 10M, 100M token tiers (Ethan)

Next steps (for AEs after meeting):
1) Fill sample prompt sheet and request 1–2 weeks logs.
2) Schedule 20-min SE demo with pre-canned dashboard + migration plan.
3) Prepare preliminary 3-month TCO delta and send follow-up one-pager.

If you want a distilled 1-slide summary for customer execs, ping me (Priya) and I’ll drop a tailored slide with numbers from the sample sheet.
